claims.text: Breiman defined random forests in Machine Learning in 2001, volume 45, pages 5 to 32, as a combination of tree predictors in which each tree depends on the values of a random vector sampled independently and with the same distribution for all trees in the forest.

source.title: Leo Breiman, Random Forests, Machine Learning 45(1):5-32, October 2001, doi 10.1023/A:1010933404324

claims.text: The central result is that the generalisation error converges almost surely to a limit as the number of trees in the forest becomes large. That limit depends on two quantities: the strength of the individual trees and the correlation between them. Using a random selection of features to split each node yields favourable error rates.

source.title: Leo Breiman, Random Forests, Machine Learning 45(1):5-32, October 2001, doi 10.1023/A:1010933404324

beats.broke: a single deep tree fits its training data almost exactly and a small change to that data produces a completely different tree, so the method is accurate in sample and unstable out of it
beats.fix: grow many trees, each on a resample and each choosing its splits from a random subset of the features, and average them — the randomisation is there to make the trees disagree with one another
beats.cost: the averaged model is no longer a rule anyone can read, and the remaining error is governed by a trade between how strong the individual trees are and how correlated they remain
beats.interview: why adding more trees to a forest does not make it overfit
